facts.title: Born in a Russian lab
facts.text: Livermorium was first created in July 2000 at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, Russia, by a team led by Yuri Oganessian. They bombarded a curium-248 target with calcium-48 ions, and a single atom of element 116 appeared and decayed within milliseconds. The discovery was the product of a long Russia-United States collaboration rather than a lone-genius moment.

facts.title: Named for a place, not a person
facts.text: The element honors the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in Livermore, California, whose scientists supplied target material and expertise for the experiments. The name was officially approved by IUPAC in May 2012, alongside flerovium for element 114. Naming an element after a town is unusual, putting Livermorium in the small club that includes berkelium, dubnium and darmstadtium.

facts.title: A truly synthetic element
facts.text: Livermorium does not occur naturally anywhere on Earth or, as far as we know, in the cosmos, because every isotope is wildly radioactive and decays almost instantly. It exists only when physicists deliberately fuse lighter nuclei in a particle accelerator. In its entire history, only a handful of atoms have ever been made.

facts.title: Gone in the blink of an eye
facts.text: The longest-lived known isotope, livermorium-293, has a half-life of only about 60 to 80 milliseconds. That is faster than a human eye blink, which takes roughly 100 to 150 milliseconds. This fleeting existence is why scientists study the element by detecting its radioactive decay products rather than ever holding a visible sample.

facts.title: Member of the oxygen family
facts.text: Livermorium sits in group 16 of the periodic table, directly below polonium, making it the heaviest known member of the chalcogen family that begins with oxygen, sulfur and selenium. Based on this position, chemists predict it could in principle form compounds resembling those of its lighter cousins. Whether it actually behaves that way is unknown, since there is never enough of it to do real chemistry.

facts.title: Relativity reshapes its electrons
facts.text: In superheavy atoms like Livermorium, the innermost electrons move at a sizeable fraction of the speed of light, so Einstein's relativity significantly alters their energy levels. These relativistic effects are predicted to make Livermorium behave less like textbook polonium than a simple periodic-table reading would suggest. Studying such elements is partly a test of how well our deepest theories of the atom hold up at the extremes.

facts.title: A stepping stone to element 117
facts.text: When scientists later created tennessine (element 117), some of its decay chains passed through isotopes of Livermorium on their way to lighter elements. In this sense Livermorium served as a recognizable signpost confirming that even heavier elements had truly been made. Reading these decay chains, like footprints, is the main way researchers prove a new superheavy element existed at all.

facts.title: Calcium-48: the magic bullet
facts.text: Livermorium is made using calcium-48, a rare, mildly radioactive isotope of calcium prized because its nucleus is doubly magic and unusually stable for fusion experiments. This isotope makes up under one percent of natural calcium and must be painstakingly enriched, making it extraordinarily expensive. Without this special projectile, creating element 116 would be far harder.

facts.title: Probing the island of stability
facts.text: Livermorium lies near a long-predicted region of the chart of nuclides called the island of stability, where certain superheavy isotopes might survive far longer than their neighbors. Each new measurement of Livermorium's isotopes helps physicists refine where that island actually sits. Confirming it would be a landmark discovery about the fundamental limits of how big an atomic nucleus can be.

facts.title: No uses, and that is the point
facts.text: Livermorium has no commercial, industrial, medical or biological applications, and it plays no role in any living organism. Its value is entirely scientific: each atom is a data point that tests our understanding of nuclear forces and the structure of matter at the heaviest extreme. Pure curiosity-driven research like this is exactly how the boundaries of the periodic table keep expanding.
